startup.name: OnDeck AI
startup.one_liner: Analyze any footage, without training a model
startup.description: Vision language model engine, Perception-0, that finds objects, behaviours or events in video with no training data. Targets enterprise and public sector customers: defense organizations, robotics research, security cameras, port monitoring and oil and gas. Six person team in Vancouver with a NeurIPS workshop paper.

yc_acceptance.basis: The input file places this company in the Summer 2025 batch, so acceptance is already known and this figure is reported for completeness only. The starting prior for a random applicant is about 1 percent (references/yc_acceptance.md, 0.6 to 2 percent third party range); the near certainty comes from the stated batch, not from a model of the company.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC is already past, so the only residual risk is a data error in the input about batch membership. Had the company been an ordinary applicant, the most plausible rejection reason would be: A crowded computer vision field where Gemini style models improve monthly, and a claim of beating the best VLMs that cannot be checked from the application.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only --industry B2B --years 2022-2024: seed known-only 61% (lower 50%, upper 68%), cond 61% (n=88). Median months to seed 9 (p25 4, p75 19); time_to_milestones.csv era 2022+ p75 is 14 months.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Window is 16 months from the as_of date to 2026-11-17. The ever anchor of 61% counts the YC deal as a seed, but this forecast counts only a financing above about $1M from outside investors that closes inside the window, so the anchor is cut to cover only rounds above $1M and only the share that close within 16 months (about 75 to 80 percent of eventual seed raisers close by month 14 to 20). Customers in defense and industry are listed in the description, which is a mild positive, but I do not lift above the anchor; the Vancouver base slightly lowers US seed access, so the net stays near 0.75 of the ever anchor. Odds are not lifted for team or hot sector, per the winners test, and do not rank this company against others.

bands.rationale: Small post YC round of $1M to $3M, usually angels or a small seed fund. Canadian and defense angels often start with a $1M to $3M check.

Institutional seed of $3M to $6M, the modal outcome in 2022 and later data (median $3.5M to $4.1M in round_benchmarks.csv, which mixes in the YC deal). The central case is a $3M to $6M seed from an AI or defense tech fund.
Larger seed of $6M to $12M, where 42 percent of confirmed 2026 raises above $1M fell in the winners test. A defense contract plus a benchmark win over Gemini could pull a $6M to $12M round.
Upside band above $12M, reserved for a standout demo with a named lead. Requires a government contract or a large enterprise win.

ladder.why_it_fails: Window of 16 months. The most likely miss is that general VLMs from Google and OpenAI improve quickly and make a specialised video model look like a feature, while defense and port customers move slowly through procurement. Visual One (AI for cameras) stopped at the YC cheque, and Traces and Aura Vision show small video AI firms that took years to raise more than $1M.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only --industry B2B --years 2022-2024: series_a cond 33% (n=54), known-only 20%; months to series A median 30 (p25 22, p75 39).
anchors.adjustment_reason: The ever anchor is 33 percent, but only about a quarter of eventual Series A raisers have closed it by month 16 (p25 is 19 to 22 months from batch start), so the windowed value is much lower. Reaching a Series A in later years is common for companies with paying customers, but it falls outside this window.

bands.rationale: Thin or bridge style Series A below the 2022 and later median of $14M to $15M, the down or flat band.
Typical Series A near the 2022 and later quartiles ($11M to $21M raise).
Upside Series A led by a top tier fund once revenue is visible; current US medians are about $17M raise on $60M pre money.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series A inside 16 months needs repeat enterprise revenue beyond pilots; the median time to Series A is about 28 months. Tenyks raised a $3.4M seed and still sold into restaurants years later, and long government sales cycles delay the round. Investors will also want proof that revenue repeats rather than comes from one defense pilot, which a company only 16 months old rarely has.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only --industry B2B --years 2022-2024: series_b cond 17% (n=18); median months to series B 46 overall, 35.5 for 2022 and later (n=40).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Median time to a Series B is about three years from batch start, so inside a 16 month window almost only extreme outliers get there; windowed probability is far below the 17 percent ever anchor.

bands.rationale: Flat or small Series B, near the 2018 to 2021 median of $32M but with a lower valuation.
Typical Series B, in line with the 2022 and later median of about $40M.
Upside Series B for a category leader; 2022 and later posts reach $600M to $1B.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series B inside 16 months would need enterprise revenue and a Series A first, and the median B2B path takes about three years from batch start (B2B median months to series B 47). Rescale, a simulation platform, took years of enterprise selling before its Series B. The likely failure is timing rather than a verdict on the idea.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only: series_c cond 36% (n=55) overall; B2B 2022-2024 cohort has 0 of 3 at Series C. Median months to series C about 61.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Series C normally lands about five years after the batch, so a window of 16 months makes it very unlikely; the ever anchor is cut to a token value.

bands.rationale: Typical Series C at the 2022 and later median of $74M.
Growth round for a scaled leader, near the 2022 and later p75 of $103M.
Upside round for a breakout company; only a few percent of YC companies get here.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series C inside 16 months is almost outside the data: the median is about five years after batch start, and only 8 companies in the 2022 and later cohort have reached it. Failing here means the company has not scaled past a niche or the window closed first, not that the idea is bad.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most paths end in a stall or a small sale because frontier labs and camera platform vendors can fold video understanding into broad products. Visual One and Sublime Black show small AI security firms that went inactive, while Tenyks and Aura Vision stayed independent and small.

analogs.relevance: Computer vision analytics sold to retailers, spun out of research.
analogs.outcome_summary: Raised about 1.1M in 2019 after YC and later won enterprise chains, staying small and independent.

analogs.relevance: Computer vision and video answering engine from a research team.
analogs.outcome_summary: Raised a 3.4M seed in March 2022, then changed markets, showing that VLM style tools find buyers slowly.
Only the 150K YC entry was found and it went inactive; depended on third party camera hardware.
Stayed active about ten staff with no priced round beyond YC found.

killers.risk: Frontier VLMs from Google and OpenAI absorb the capability, leaving no moat for a specialised layer.
killers.evidence: The description itself compares against Gemini, and general models improve quickly on video benchmarks.
killers.mitigation: Own the deployment layer for long footage and on premise defense use.

killers.risk: Defense and port customers have slow procurement so revenue stays at pilots.
killers.evidence: National defense customers are listed, and procurement is long; AI video analytics is a $5B to $15B market but fragmented.
killers.mitigation: Sign paid pilots with a prime contractor.

killers.risk: Camera platform vendors bundle analytics for free.
killers.evidence: Security camera vendors and video platforms embed analytics in hardware.
killers.mitigation: Focus on the hard long video events they cannot detect.

competition_now.name: Video analytics vendors and camera makers
competition_now.traction: AI video analytics estimated at about $5B to $15B in 2025 depending on definition.

competition_now.name: AI in video surveillance suppliers
competition_now.what: Surveillance analytics with detection models that need training data.
competition_now.traction: Large market with many regional vendors.

competition_now.name: Status quo: trained custom vision models
competition_now.what: Teams collect data and train a model per task.
competition_now.traction: Takes months, the pain the company cites.

technical_complexity.rationale: Long video understanding with VLMs at low cost needs both model work and efficient inference; six people can ship a working engine but lag frontier labs in scale of training and evaluation.

takeover_risk.rationale: General multimodal models already read video, so a competing feature within 9 months is plausible; the startup differs through long footage handling and deployment in sensitive settings.

evidence.claim: AI video analytics is estimated between about $5B and $15B in 2025 by different reports.
Zero shot detection is described as letting operators search in plain language instead of labeling data, a single vendor estimate of a small but fast growing niche.

roadmap.goal: A public benchmark win on long video understanding.
actions: Publish results against Gemini on a named dataset.
Open a demo for defense and port teams.
roadmap.proof: A benchmark table and two letters of intent.

roadmap.goal: Paid pilots that support a $3M to $6M seed.
actions: Convert a defense or port pilot to paid.
Get a security accreditation for government work.

pros.point: Named enterprise and defense customers at batch start.
pros.evidence: Description lists defense, robotics, security and port monitoring customers.

pros.point: A research paper and a working model, with six people.
pros.evidence: NeurIPS workshop paper is stated in the input.

brand.name: OnDeck AI
brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "OnDeck AI" --era 2022+: name_plus_descriptor, camel_case, cohort alive 93.7%, n=557
weaknesses: Shares a name with an unrelated well known fintech and carries an AI descriptor
brand.rationale: The AI suffix is a generic tag many YC names use; the name collides with other companies called OnDeck in search, a real cost for findability, but B2B buyers weigh proof over names.

narrative.headline: Real early customers but a fast moving field; 45 percent for a seed above $1M in 16 months.
narrative.general_summary: OnDeck sells a vision language model engine for video, with early defense and industrial customers and a six person team. The market is large, and a model that needs no training data is attractive, but frontier labs are improving video understanding quickly and procurement is slow. Inside a 16 month window a seed above $1M is slightly under the cohort anchor, adjusted down only for the window, and a Series A in the window is unlikely. The ladder does not rank this company above others. The biggest failure path is that general models become good enough that buyers see this as a feature.

assumptions: Customer list and the benchmark claim come from the company description and are unverified.
Blind forecast made as of 2025-07-07 for the window to 2026-11-17 (16 months). Seed means an outside round above about $1M closing in the window, not the standard YC deal of about $500K.
Coverage limit: 662 of 6,399 companies are researched, and the B2B 2022-2024 cohort has 107 companies, so cohort rates are wide.
Probabilities do not rank this company against others; the winners test found no separation between raisers and non-raisers.
